newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - brokers, promoters charged in bribe schemes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - brokers, promoters charged in bribe schemes.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

A far-flung group of stock promoters, brokers, and company officers were charged Thursday with participating in bribery schemes marking the largest set of arrests ever in the securities industry, federal authorities said.

Forty-five defendants were named in nineteen separate criminal complaints alleging that stock promoters and officers of publicly-traded companies bribed brokers to induce customers to buy low-priced stocks.

Mary Jo White, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, said 36 of the defendants have so far been taken into custody "in the largest single set of arrests ever made in the securities industry."
The charges were also unusual because they stemmed from an unprecedented FBI undercover operation in which federal agents posed as stock brokers willing to take bribes.
Most of the defendants in the far flung schemes are stock promoters and they live in Florida, California, Arizona, Utah, Illinois, Colorado, Canada, New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.
In addition to the criminal charges, the Securities and Exchange Commission filed civil suits against 28 of the defendants.
White told a news conference that the success of the undercover sting operation underscores the pervasiveness of this kind of illegal activity.

She said that the eventual arrest of all 45 defendants in itself is a "staggering event." However she said this number is just the "tip of the iceberg" as the investigation is continuing and more arrests are expected.
"The evidence revealed...a sordid picture of greed and indifference to the investing public," White said.
She said hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash and stock payments were offered to brokers.
White said the fact that most of the defendants had no connection to each other was further proof that such illegal payoff schemes are widespread.

James Kallstrom, who heads the FBI's New York office, said that while authorities cannot quantify how widespread the practice is "I'll tell you this, we didn't have to wait around very long until alot of people would beat our doors down to do these types of deals. There was an avalanche of people out there"
He said the FBI agents posed as "unscrupulous brokers" who managed millions of dollars on behalf of supposed "high net worth individuals."
The undercover brokers were willing to accept payoffs to sell "penny" or low-priced stocks, often valued at under $5 per share and traded in over-the-counter markets, to their customers.

The payments were generally made by and through stock promoters who, working often with officers of the companies whose stocks were being touted, paid the brokers as much as 40 percent of the value of the stock being sold to the brokers' customers.
The criminal charges include conspiracy, securities fraud, and criminal contempt.
If convicted, the defendants in the criminal cases face sentences of between five and 50 years and fines of up to $250,000 per count.
The SEC civil suits are seeking court orders prohibiting the defendants from promoting penny stocks and repayment of illegal profits.

"Today's arrests should send a clear and unambiguous message to unscrupulous stock promoters, stock brokers and officers of publicly traded companies. The gloves are off in the fight to protect the nation's financial markets," White said.
A number of the promoters were former brokers who were the subject of regulatory or court orders, she added.

William McLucas, the SEC's director of enforcement, said his theory is that many of the defendants are "professional follow-the-con" people who were involved in penny stock fraud 10 years ago then moved on to internet fraud and are now taking advantage of the immense amount of money flowing into the stock market.
